\chapter{Review --- Four Verbs of the Mind}
\label{ch:spanish-review-verbs-of-mind}
\hlchaptermodality{152}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can hold all four mind-verbs at once and name the physical act inside each one.}

Four abstractions, four labourers: weighing, stretching, gathering, scratching.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[Practice]{Review — four verbs of the mind}

\label{lesson:ES-C34-repaso-mente}



\begin{quote}
Nothing new in this chapter. Name the four verbs of the last four chapters: to think, to understand, to read, to write.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
Here is the thing none of the four chapters could show you on its own.

Every one of these four \textquotedblleft{}mental\textquotedblright{} verbs began as something you do with your \textbf{body}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{pensar} — Latin \emph{pēnsāre}, to \textbf{weigh}. Thinking is putting things on a balance. English kept the scales in \emph{weigh your options}, and in \emph{pensive}.
  \item \textbf{entender} — Latin \emph{intendere}, to \textbf{stretch toward}. Understanding is reaching. English kept the reach in \emph{attention}.
  \item \textbf{leer} — Latin \emph{legere}, to \textbf{gather, pick out}. Reading is picking grain from a field. English kept the gathering in \emph{collect}, \emph{select}, \emph{elect}.
  \item \textbf{escribir} — Latin \emph{scrībere}, to \textbf{scratch}. Writing is scratching a surface, which is exactly what it was.
\end{itemize}

Four abstractions, four labourers. No language invents a word for thinking; it borrows one from the hands and lets the meaning drift indoors.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{And a hidden joint.} \emph{Intellect} is Latin \emph{inter} + \emph{legere} — \textquotedblleft{}to gather \textbf{between}.\textquotedblright{} The root of \textbf{leer} is sitting inside the English word for the mind itself.
\end{quote}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four verbs, and with them the four things you do with a language: take it in (\emph{leer}), work on it (\emph{pensar}), get it (\emph{entender}), put it back out (\emph{escribir}).
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the four verbs in order — to read, to think, to understand, to write
  \item for each one, the body word underneath it
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{entender} physically mean? (\textbf{To stretch toward}.) What do all four have in common? (Each was a \textbf{body} word before it was a mind word.) Next chapter you will use them to say something you actually think.
\end{tcolorbox}
